narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though with less force. Surprisingly, your undergraduate GPA was the only factor that pulled slightly in the positive direction, yet it was not enough to overcome the other signals.

Compared with students who were admitted, you ranked much lower in your class both in year one (2nd decile versus an average of 6th) and especially in year three (1st decile versus an average near 6th). Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.5 were also well below the averages of accepted students (37 and 3.23 respectively). Your upper-middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
